as_told: In the 1920s researchers at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works near Chicago changed the lighting to see how it affected the workers' output. Output went up when the light was made brighter, and it also went up when the light was made dimmer. The researchers concluded that the workers worked harder simply because they were being watched.
lesson: People work harder or change their behaviour simply because they know they are being observed (the 'Hawthorne effect').
what_happened: The illumination tests ran from November 1924 to April 1927 and were led for the National Research Council by C. E. Snow. In the first test, output 'bobbed up and down' without a clear link to the light. In the second test, output rose in both the test group and the control group by almost the same amount. In the third test, output rose in both groups as the test group's light was lowered, but when it reached 3 foot-candles the workers protested that they could hardly see, and output fell. The company concluded only that light was a minor factor and that too many other factors were uncontrolled; it did not conclude that being watched raised output. When Levitt and List found and analysed the surviving data in 2009, they found that the famous descriptions of the data were not true, with only faint signs of an effect of being studied.
false_part: Output did not rise whatever the lighting change (it fell when the light became too dim), and the researchers did not show that being watched caused the rises; they said the test was not controlled well enough to tell.

earliest_telling.who: F. J. Roethlisberger and William J. Dickson
earliest_telling.where: Management and the Worker (Harvard University Press), chapter I, 'Experiments on Illumination', p. 17
earliest_telling.quote: Even with this very low intensity of light, the girls maintained their efficiency.

original.what: C. E. Snow's report on the second illumination test, 'A Discussion of the Relation of Illumination Intensity to Productive Efficiency', The Tech Engineering News, November 1927, as quoted in Roethlisberger and Dickson, Management and the Worker (1939), p. 16
original.quote: This test resulted in very appreciable production increases in both groups and of almost identical magnitude.

original.what: Snow's report on the third illumination test, as quoted in Roethlisberger and Dickson (1939), pp. 16-17
original.quote: the operatives protested, saying that they were hardly able to see what they were doing, and the production rate decreased.

original.what: The company's own conclusion from the illumination tests, in the official account of the Hawthorne research by Roethlisberger (Harvard) and Dickson (Western Electric), Management and the Worker (1939), p. 18
original.who: F. J. Roethlisberger and William J. Dickson
original.quote: that light is only one, and apparently a minor, factor among many which affect employee output;

original.what: Analysis of the recovered data of the illumination tests: Levitt and List, 'Was There Really a Hawthorne Effect at the Hawthorne Plant? An Analysis of the Original Illumination Experiments', NBER Working Paper 15016 (May 2009); published in American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 2011
original.who: Steven D. Levitt and John A. List
original.quote: We find that existing descriptions of supposedly remarkable data patterns prove to be entirely fictional.

lesson_verdict.why: A systematic review of studies across all fields found that taking part in research does change behaviour in some studies, but that little can be known securely about when this happens, how it works or how large it is.

source.what: McCambridge, Witton and Elbourne, 'Systematic review of the Hawthorne effect: New concepts are needed to study research participation effects', Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 67(3):267-277 (2014)
source.quote: Consequences of research participation for behaviors being investigated do exist, although little can be securely known about the conditions under which they operate, their mechanisms of effects, or their magnitudes.

search_steps: Open Library full-text search for "Hawthorne" "illumination" "control group" "output": 8,943 hits; the earliest were Roethlisberger, Management and Morale (scan of a 1946 printing of the 1941 book; borrow-only, not saved) and Urwick and Brech, The Making of Scientific Management, vol. III (1948; full text, saved).

Urwick and Brech 1948 (pp. 15-16, note 2) quote a livelier popular telling from a Reader's Digest article of April 1941, 'What Makes the Worker Like to Work?': 'the output of the control group without a single candlepower of extra light went up too'. I could not find that article online. It is later than the 1939 book, so it is not the earliest telling.

Archive.org search: saved the full text of Roethlisberger and Dickson, Management and the Worker (1939), the earliest telling I could read; it quotes Snow's 1927 report on the three tests and describes the two workers who kept their output at moonlight level. Mayo, The Human Problems of an Industrial Civilization (1933), exists on archive.org only as a borrow-only scan; not read.
C. E. Snow's own article (The Tech Engineering News, November 1927) was not found online; it is quoted here only through Roethlisberger and Dickson, who print it as Snow's words.
Saved Levitt and List, NBER Working Paper 15016 (2009), which analyses the recovered original data.
The phrase 'Hawthorne effect' and the explanation 'because they were watched' do not appear in the 1939 account; I did not find or save the first use of the phrase.
Lesson source: saved McCambridge et al. 2014 from PubMed Central (PMC3969247).

HathiTrust and Google Books full-text search: HathiTrust refused with a Cloudflare check; Google Books API refused with 429; did not retry. Chronicling America refused with 403 and Papers Past with a bot check; did not retry.
confidence_note: Snow's 1927 report is known only from the long quotations in Roethlisberger and Dickson. Snow's 1927 article and Mayo's 1933 book may tell the story earlier than 1939, but I could not read them. The NBER file I saved has 10 pages and may be a short version of the paper.
